title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon (Alfama) ⚡ Map Routing
description: Watch Greedy Best-First choose the next street segment using only a heuristic to the goal—fast, but not always optimal. This visualization connects street-map graph search to real software engineering and system design decisions.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First tech + artificial intelligence routing in Lisbon streets—see the algorithms choose the next hop fast.

In this Lisbon (Alfama) pathfinding visualization, we model the map as a graph: intersections are nodes, streets are edges, and each node carries coordinates for distance estimates. Greedy Best-First uses a priority queue ordered by a heuristic h(n) = estimated cost from node n to the goal (e.g., straight-line distance). At every step, it expands the single most promising frontier node—ignoring the path cost so far (unlike A*).

That’s the core tradeoff: Greedy Best-First is often quick because it chases the goal aggressively, but it can get misled by misleading heuristics (like steep hills, cul-de-sacs, or map geometry) and may produce longer routes.

Engineering takeaway: when designing AI for navigation, think about heuristic quality, tie-breaking, and failure cases—then add guardrails (e.g., fallback search, bounded exploration) as part of system design.

Which is more important for your use case: fastest-first routes or guaranteed near-optimal paths? Drop your take—Greedy vs A*—in the comments.
